code.title: Venv: prefix vs base_prefix and sys.path

followUps:
Because the venv stores absolute paths to the interpreter it was created from and to itself. pyvenv.cfg has a home line, and scripts in bin/ start with a shebang like #!/proj/.venv/bin/python.

If you move /proj to /work, those paths point nowhere and the scripts break. The fix is cheap: delete the venv and recreate it from the lock file. Treat venvs as disposable, never as something you copy or commit.

Conda is a full package manager that installs binaries of any language, including Python itself and C libraries, while venv only isolates Python packages for an interpreter that already exists.

A conda environment can hold its own Python 3.11, its own OpenSSL and CUDA, all from conda channels. A venv with pip cannot supply a system library. That is why data science stacks often use conda, and web services use venv or uv. Mixing pip inside conda works but can leave conflicting files, so install with conda first and pip last.

It lets the venv also see the packages installed in the base Python's site-packages; the default is false, which gives a clean, isolated environment.

When it is true, pyvenv.cfg says include-system-site-packages = true and the base site-packages is added after the venv's own on sys.path. Example: an OS package python3-numpy becomes importable inside the venv without reinstalling. The cost is that your project now depends on whatever the OS has, which hurts reproducibility.

code.title: Why an install does not import: first match on sys.path

followUps:
PEP 668 lets a distribution mark its Python as externally managed, so pip install outside a venv fails with an externally-managed-environment error instead of overwriting files owned by apt or dnf.

The marker is an EXTERNALLY-MANAGED file in the standard library folder. The sensible reaction is to create a venv (python -m venv .venv), or use pipx or uv tool install for command-line tools. --break-system-packages exists but can break OS tools that are written in Python.

Make the correct way the only way: one project-local environment created by a single command, and never a bare pip.

  • Commit a lock file and a one-line setup, for example uv sync or make venv.
  • Run everything through uv run or .venv/bin/python -m ..., so the interpreter is explicit.
  • Use a pinned .python-version, and set PIP_REQUIRE_VIRTUALENV=1 so global installs fail.
  • CI runs the same command, so a mismatch shows up on the first pull request.

code.title: Reading wheel names versus sdists
code.python:
# Parse wheel file names and tell wheels from sdists.
def parse_wheel(fn):
    parts = fn[:-4].split("-")             # strip ".whl"
    name, version = parts[0], parts[1]
    py, abi, plat = parts[-3:]
    return name, version, py, abi, plat

files = [
    "numpy-2.0.0-cp312-cp312-manylinux_2_28_x86_64.whl",
    "requests-2.32.3-py3-none-any.whl",
    "legacy-1.0.tar.gz",
]
for f in files:
    if f.endswith(".whl"):
        n, v, py, abi, plat = parse_wheel(f)
        pure = (abi, plat) == ("none", "any")
        print(f"{f}\n  wheel: {n} {v} python={py} abi={abi} platform={plat}")
        print("  ->", "pure Python, works anywhere" if pure else "compiled, platform specific")
        print("  -> install = unpack files, no code runs")
    else:
        print(f"{f}\n  sdist: pip must build a wheel first (runs build backend)")

followUps:
It guarantees that the wheel only needs system libraries that exist in a Linux distribution with glibc 2.28 or newer, so it runs on Debian 10, Ubuntu 18.10, RHEL 8 and anything newer.

The tag encodes the glibc version it was built against: manylinux_2_28 means glibc 2.28. Tools like auditwheel check that the compiled files link only to an allowed list of libraries and symbols, and bundle the rest inside the wheel. A machine with glibc 2.17 would refuse it. Alpine uses musl, so it needs musllinux wheels instead.

The stable ABI (abi3) is a limited set of CPython C-API functions that keep the same binary interface across versions, so one compiled wheel works on many Python versions.

A wheel tagged cp39-abi3-manylinux_2_17_x86_64 runs on Python 3.9, 3.10, 3.11, 3.12 and later, because the extension used only the limited API. The trade-off is that some fast internals are unavailable, so it can be a little slower. Projects use it to ship one wheel per platform rather than one per Python version.

Use it when the build needs packages that are already installed in the current environment, or when you cannot download the build requirements, for example in an offline or pinned build.

By default pip builds in a fresh isolated environment with the packages from [build-system].requires. With --no-build-isolation it builds in your current environment instead. You must then install the build tools yourself (pip install setuptools wheel). It is also used to build against a specific installed NumPy. The risk is that the build now depends on whatever is in the environment.

code.title: Parsing pyproject.toml sections with tomllib
code.python:
# Read the main sections of a pyproject.toml with the standard tomllib (Python 3.11+).
import tomllib

TEXT = """
[build-system]
requires = ["hatchling"]
build-backend = "hatchling.build"

[project]
name = "demo"
version = "0.1.0"
requires-python = ">=3.9"
dependencies = ["requests>=2.31"]

[project.optional-dependencies]
cli = ["click>=8"]

[project.scripts]
demo = "demo.main:run"

[dependency-groups]
dev = ["pytest", "ruff"]

[tool.ruff]
line-length = 100
"""
data = tomllib.loads(TEXT)
print("top-level tables:", list(data))
print("backend:", data["build-system"]["build-backend"])
p = data["project"]
print("published deps:", p["dependencies"])
print("extras (published):", p["optional-dependencies"])
print("console script:", p["scripts"])
print("dev group (not published):", data["dependency-groups"]["dev"])
print("tool config:", data["tool"]["ruff"])

followUps:
Only when you must run custom build logic that the pyproject backend cannot express, or when a tool still reads it. For ordinary pure Python packages it is no longer needed.

Examples: a legacy project with no [build-system] table, old tools that run python setup.py develop, or a build that compiles C code with custom steps using setuptools. Even then, keep metadata in [project] and use setup.py only for the extension logic, such as setup(ext_modules=[...]). Running python setup.py install directly is deprecated.

Extras are published and chosen by the end user; dependency groups are for developers and are never published.

Use an extra when a feature is optional for users: pip install demo[cli] pulls in click. Use a dependency group (PEP 735) for tools that only contributors need, such as dev = ["pytest", "ruff"], installed with uv sync --group dev. Groups do not appear in the package metadata, so users never see or install them. Rule of thumb: if the installed package itself needs it, an extra; if only the repo needs it, a group.

code.title: A backtracking dependency resolver
code.python:
# A tiny backtracking resolver: pick newest version, backtrack on conflict.
INDEX = {  # package -> version -> {dependency: allowed versions}
    "app":  {1: {"lib": {1, 2, 3}, "util": {1}}},
    "lib":  {3: {"util": {2}}, 2: {"util": {1, 2}}, 1: {"util": {1}}},
    "util": {2: {}, 1: {}},
}

def resolve(todo, chosen):
    if not todo:
        return chosen
    pkg, allowed = todo[0]
    if pkg in chosen:
        return resolve(todo[1:], chosen) if chosen[pkg] in allowed else None
    for v in sorted(INDEX[pkg], reverse=True):      # newest first
        if v not in allowed:
            continue
        print("  try", pkg, v)
        deps = [(d, a) for d, a in INDEX[pkg][v].items()]
        res = resolve(deps + todo[1:], {**chosen, pkg: v})
        if res:
            return res
        print("  backtrack from", pkg, v)
    return None

print("requirements: app 1")
print("result:", resolve([("app", {1})], {}))

followUps:
Finding the best set of versions can be shown to be as hard as the satisfiability problem, which is NP-complete, because every package may have many versions and each version picks different dependency ranges.

In the worst case a resolver might try every combination: 3 packages with 10 versions each means 10 x 10 x 10 = 1000 combinations, and with 30 packages that is 1030. Real resolvers stay fast because they prune early with learned conflicts (PubGrub) and because most packages have loose, compatible ranges. Bad lower bounds are what make them slow in practice.

-r means install these packages; -c only limits which versions are allowed if a package is needed, and installs nothing by itself.

With -r requirements.txt containing requests, pip installs requests. With -c constraints.txt containing urllib3<2 and requests requested, urllib3 is installed only because requests needs it, and it will be below 2. Constraints are handy for a shared version policy across many projects, and for steering the resolver after a conflict.

code.title: Declared ranges versus a full lock

followUps:
Caret constraints such as ^1.2 in Poetry also add an upper bound (<2.0), and in a library that bound is passed on to everyone who installs it.

Say your library needs foo>=1.2,<2.0 and another library needs foo>=2.0. The user cannot install both, even if your code works fine with foo 2.0. Upper bounds guess the future, and they block users from getting fixes. Libraries should set an upper bound only for a known break, and application locks should do the pinning.

Let a bot propose the updates as pull requests, and let CI decide whether they are safe.

  1. Run Dependabot or Renovate weekly; group minor and patch bumps into one pull request.
  2. CI installs from the new lock and runs the full tests, plus pip-audit.
  3. Read the lock diff for new transitive packages.
  4. Use a cooldown (for example, skip versions younger than 7 days) to avoid freshly compromised releases.

Security fixes merge fast; big major bumps get a person to review.

A universal lock file is one lock that is valid for every platform and Python version you support, not just the machine that created it.

The resolver records separate entries where they differ, using markers, for example pywin32; sys_platform == "win32" or a numpy 1.x pin for Python 3.8 and 2.x for 3.12. Running uv lock on a Mac therefore gives the same lock that Linux CI and a Windows laptop use. A pip-compile file, by contrast, is solved for one platform and one Python only.

Do it in small steps, since the formats are close now that both use the standard [project] table.

  1. For Poetry 1.x to 2, run poetry check, move [tool.poetry.dependencies] into [project] (caret ranges become explicit ranges), then re-lock.
  2. For uv, keep the [project] table, run uv lock and uv sync, and compare the resolved versions with the old lock.
  3. Change CI and Docker commands, then delete the old lock file.

Check that the test suite passes on the new lock before merging.

code.title: src layout hides missing-install bugs
code.python:
# Why the src layout catches packaging bugs: imports from the project root succeed
# only when the package sits there, hiding the fact it is not installed.
def can_import(name, path, fs):
    return any(name in fs.get(d, []) for d in path)

flat = {"/repo": ["pkg", "tests"], "/site-packages": []}            # not installed
src  = {"/repo": ["src", "tests"], "/site-packages": []}            # not installed
path = ["/repo", "/site-packages"]       # running tests puts the repo root first

print("flat layout, package NOT installed:", can_import("pkg", path, flat))
print("src layout,  package NOT installed:", can_import("pkg", path, src))

src["/site-packages"].append("pkg")      # pip install -e . or normal install
print("src layout,  after install        :", can_import("pkg", path, src))

# Editable install via a .pth file: each line is added to sys.path at startup.
pth = "/repo/src"
path.append(pth)
src[pth] = ["pkg"]
print("editable .pth adds:", pth, "->", can_import("pkg", path, src))

followUps:
Because an import-hook editable install adds no real path to src/ that a static tool can read; the mapping lives in a finder object that only exists when Python runs.

mypy and Pyright resolve imports by searching directories and .pth entries. A hook-based install (for example setuptools in strict mode) only leaves a small file that registers a finder at startup, so the checker reports Cannot find implementation or library stub for module named pkg. Fixes: use the .pth-style editable mode (hatch default, uv), set mypy_path = "src", or pass --config-settings editable_mode=compat to pip.

python -P (Python 3.11 and later) stops Python from adding the script's folder, or the current folder, to the front of sys.path.

Without it, python script.py puts the script's directory first, so a local requests.py or pkg/ directory can shadow the installed package. With -P (or PYTHONSAFEPATH=1) that folder is left out, which makes tests use the installed package and prevents accidental imports of local files. It is a good setting for CI.

Do not turn it on everywhere at once; start with a baseline, then ratchet upward.

  1. Add mypy with lenient defaults and ignore_missing_imports and get a green run.
  2. Turn on strict mode per package: [[tool.mypy.overrides]] module = "billing.*" strict = true.
  3. Require types in all new files, and in files you edit.
  4. Track the error count in CI so it only goes down.

Start with the most stable, most imported modules. Tools like monkeytype can propose annotations.

The team runs one tool instead of three, it is much faster, and the formatting is almost the same as Black.

Ruff is written in Rust and checks a big repo in about a second, where flake8 plus isort plus Black can take 10 to 30 seconds. One config table replaces .flake8, isort settings and black settings. Expect some small formatting differences from Black, a one-time reformat commit (add its hash to .git-blame-ignore-revs), and rules to choose via select. Plugins that Ruff does not have are the only reason to keep flake8.

Yanking hides a release from new resolution but does not break anyone who pinned that exact version.

If your lock says pkg==1.2.0 and 1.2.0 is yanked, pip still installs 1.2.0, because the exact pin is a deliberate request (PEP 592). Someone with pkg>=1.0 will skip 1.2.0 and pick another version. Yanking is therefore the right tool for a broken release, while deleting is not allowed to reuse a version. Always upload a fixed 1.2.1 afterwards.

Build the wheels on each operating system in CI, and publish all of them together with the sdist in a single release.

For pure Python code, one py3-none-any wheel is enough. For compiled code, run cibuildwheel in a matrix of Linux (manylinux and musllinux), macOS (x86_64 and arm64) and Windows runners, with one wheel for each supported Python version (or one abi3 wheel). Upload all files as artifacts, then a final job downloads them and publishes with Trusted Publishing. Test an install of each wheel before upload.

code.title: Reproducible archives need fixed timestamps
code.python:
# Reproducible builds: the same inputs must give byte-identical archives.
import hashlib, io, zipfile

def build(files, fixed_time):
    buf = io.BytesIO()
    with zipfile.ZipFile(buf, "w") as z:
        for name in sorted(files):                       # stable order
            info = zipfile.ZipInfo(name, date_time=fixed_time)
            z.writestr(info, files[name])
    return hashlib.sha256(buf.getvalue()).hexdigest()[:16]

files = {"pkg/__init__.py": "x = 1\n", "pkg/mod.py": "def f(): return 2\n"}
epoch = (2020, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0)                            # like SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH
print("fixed time, build 1:", build(files, epoch))
print("fixed time, build 2:", build(files, epoch))
a = build(files, (2024, 5, 1, 9, 0, 0))                # build run at one time
b = build(files, (2024, 5, 1, 9, 0, 10))               # same inputs, later clock
print("same hash with real clock times:", a == b, "(timestamps leak in)")

followUps:
Quite a lot: the operating system, CPU architecture, system libraries, and anything that reads the clock or the network at build time.

Even with a pinned lock and digest, a base image tag like python:3.12 moves unless you use the digest. Wheels contain timestamps and file order unless SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH is set. Compiled extensions can differ by compiler version and flags, and an sdist build may download extra files. Check by building twice and comparing sha256sum of the output; if the hashes differ, diffoscope shows which file changed.

Because the package cache holds the downloaded wheels, which are the same for any environment with the same lock, while a venv contains absolute paths and compiled files tied to one Python and one OS.

Restoring a cache of 300 MB of wheels and running uv sync takes seconds and always builds a correct, fresh venv. A cached venv can contain a stale package left over from an old lock, or paths that no longer match the runner. Key the cache on the lock hash, Python version and OS.

code.title: Dependency confusion across indexes

followUps:
You mostly get the real risk from the --extra-index-url behaviour: the highest version across all indexes wins, so a public package with a higher version can replace an internal one.

Walk through the case: your internal acme-internal 1.4.0 and a public acme-internal 99.0.0. An installer that searches both indexes picks 99.0.0 and runs its build or install code with your credentials. Defences: one controlled index, an explicit package-to-index pin, hashes in the lock, and reserving your internal names on the public index.

An attestation (PEP 740) proves that a file was built from a certain source repository and workflow and uploaded by it; it does not prove the code is safe.

It is a signed statement, created by Trusted Publishing, that says: this wheel with this SHA-256 came from this repository, commit and GitHub Actions workflow. A consumer can verify that the file was not swapped later. It says nothing about the author's intent: a compromised repository or a malicious maintainer still produces a validly attested malicious release. So combine it with review, pinning and auditing.

code.title: Choosing a wheel from compatibility tags
code.python:
# Choose among wheels: the interpreter's ordered tag list; first tag with a wheel wins.
SUPPORTED = [  # most specific first, like packaging.tags.sys_tags()
    "cp312-cp312-manylinux_2_28_x86_64",
    "cp312-cp312-manylinux_2_17_x86_64",
    "cp312-abi3-manylinux_2_17_x86_64",
    "cp311-abi3-manylinux_2_17_x86_64",
    "cp312-none-any",
    "py3-none-any",
]

def expand(tag):                       # "py2.py3-none-any" -> two tags
    py, abi, plat = tag.split("-")
    return [f"{p}-{abi}-{plat}" for p in py.split(".")]

def pick(wheel_tags):
    best = None
    for w in wheel_tags:
        for t in expand(w):
            if t in SUPPORTED:
                rank = SUPPORTED.index(t)
                if best is None or rank < best[0]:
                    best = (rank, w)
    return best[1] if best else "no wheel -> build sdist"

print("pure:", pick(["py2.py3-none-any"]))
print("abi3:", pick(["cp311-abi3-manylinux_2_17_x86_64", "py3-none-any"]))
print("both:", pick(["cp312-cp312-manylinux_2_28_x86_64", "py3-none-any"]))
print("musl:", pick(["cp312-cp312-musllinux_1_2_x86_64"]))

followUps:
Because Alpine Linux uses musl instead of glibc, and most projects publish only manylinux (glibc) wheels, so pip finds no matching wheel and falls back to the sdist.

Then pip must compile, which needs gcc, headers and minutes of time: for example, installing numpy or cryptography from source can take 5 to 20 minutes. If a musllinux wheel exists, no build happens. Often the simplest fix is a -slim Debian-based image instead of Alpine.

An abi3 wheel is compiled only against the limited, stable C-API, and its tag names the oldest Python it supports, so any newer Python can use it.

The tag cp39-abi3-win_amd64 is accepted by Python 3.9, 3.10, 3.11 and later on Windows x86-64. In the installer's tag list you see cp312-abi3, cp311-abi3, down to cp39-abi3, so a Python 3.12 interpreter matches it. That is why the example program ranks cp311-abi3 above plain py3-none-any. The wheel is built once instead of once per Python version.

Watch for the output line "Building wheel" or "Running setup.py" in the install log, or ban the fallback so it fails loudly.

Use pip install --only-binary :all: -r requirements.txt, or uv sync --no-build; an sdist-only package then raises an error naming it. For a lighter check, run pip install -v and search the log for Building wheel for, or compare install time per package. List exceptions explicitly with --no-binary pkg. Fix by upgrading to a version with wheels or building one into a private index.

The main risk is a stale or wrong environment being restored as if it were correct, plus a larger cache and possible leaks of secrets.

A venv restored from an old key can contain removed packages, so tests pass in CI but fail in a clean install. Venvs also hold absolute paths and compiled code tied to one Python build, so a runner image update silently breaks them. They are big (hundreds of MB), slow to upload, and may include tokens in config. Cache the downloads instead, and key on the lock hash.
